extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and novelists learning to use unreliable narrators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting and employing unreliable narrators in fiction, including types, techniques for planting clues, voice development, and how to use the device to create misdirection and reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of an unreliable narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: An unreliable narrator is a character who tells the story but cannot be trusted to provide an accurate or complete account of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unreliability can result from personal bias, mental instability, deliberate deception, or a lack of knowledge. Understanding the cause of unreliability is central to deploying the technique effectively because it shapes how and why the narrator distorts the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberately deceptive narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator who intentionally lies or manipulates information to serve their own purposes or to mislead readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Gone Girl's Amy Dunne fabricates her disappearance and leaves a diary to point suspicion elsewhere. This type can also lie to protect someone they respect or feel responsible for (the guide cites The Great Gatsby's Nick Carraway as an instance where closeness and admiration color the account). Use deliberate deception to create striking misdirection and plot twists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentally unstable narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator whose mental illness or instability causes them to perceive events inaccurately or to convey a distorted version of reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Holden Caulfield in The Catcher in the Rye — his unstable perspective forces readers to sift through subjective accounts to find truth. Use hallucinations, paranoia, unreliable memories, or distorted perception as mechanisms for unreliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naïve or innocent narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator who is inexperienced, naïve, or innocent and therefore misunderstands or misinterprets events, leading to an incomplete or inaccurate account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Scout Finch in To Kill a Mockingbird — a limited perspective means readers must infer broader social realities from the narrator's observations. This type works well when the narrator's limited knowledge is believable and integral to the story's perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subvert genre conventions and obligatory moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand how to use and subvert the CONVENTIONS and OBLIGATORY MOMENTS of your genre to create mystery and uncertainty within your narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately playing against expected genre beats can heighten suspense and make the narrator's unreliability more destabilizing. Know the reader's expectations and then withhold, twist, or falsify what would normally be an 'obligatory' moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan placement of subtle clues
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate subtle clues throughout your story that hint at the narrator’s unreliability (inconsistencies, other characters questioning credibility, moments of self-doubt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the location of each clue to create a balance between reality and falsehoods; scatter evidence thoughtfully so readers can, in retrospect, piece together the true story. The guide references planning tools like the Story Grid’s NARRATIVE PATH to map this out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish an authentic voice and journey for the narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the narrator a relatable, engaging character with a unique and compelling voice even while their account is unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humanize the narrator with moments of vulnerability, sincerity, or insight so readers feel emotionally invested despite doubts about veracity. A strong, believable voice prevents the technique from feeling like a gimmick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use unreliability to subvert reader expectations and create twists
rubrics_metrics.description: Present a version of events that is later revealed to be false or incomplete to create surprising twists and keep the audience guessing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This effect can be achieved in multiple ways; the guide highlights that subverting expectations is one of the most powerful uses of an unreliable narrator. Ensure the reveal is supported by prior clues so the twist feels earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invite readers to be active participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the unreliable narrator to engage readers in deciphering the truth from the character’s biased or distorted account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the narrative so readers must piece together the puzzle and draw their own conclusions, creating a more immersive and interactive reading experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from examples of unreliable narrators
rubrics_metrics.description: Study literary examples (e.g., Humbert Humbert in Lolita; Patrick Bateman in American Psycho; Chief Bromden in One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest; Nelly Dean in Wuthering Heights) to see different manifestations of unreliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how each example's unreliability—manipulation, delusion, paranoia, bias—affects tone, reader sympathy, and plot structure. Use these case studies as models for tone, voice, and how to balance empathy with deception.
